query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An isothermal aging treatment at 700°C for 1 hour under an inert atmosphere will promote the in situ formation of a homogeneously dispersed population of fine sigma precipitates in a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature yield strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in the as-cast or solution-treated state exhibiting a single-phase BCC matrix with minimal pre-existing precipitates.
generation.intervention: Apply an isothermal aging treatment at 700°C for 1 hour under an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon).
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (up to 700°C) after treatment; the alloy’s composition must adhere to the high-entropy criteria (five or more elements, with titanium and nickel as primary constituents) and be processed under inert conditions to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a homogeneous distribution of fine sigma precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation hardening via sigma precipitates that impede dislocation motion and stabilize grain boundaries, which collectively contribute to an increased yield strength at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit a higher yield strength and improved mechanical stability at elevated temperatures (up to 700°C) compared to its untreated counterpart.
generation.baseline: The untreated (as-cast or solution-treated) alloy with a single-phase BCC structure lacking the fine sigma precipitate dispersion, leading to relatively lower high-temperature strength.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under the specified treatment conditions and for alloys within the defined compositional window (titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys). The hypothesis is limited to performance enhancements at temperatures up to 700°C.
generation.uncertainty: The precise precipitate volume fraction, their size distribution, and the quantitative contribution of these precipitates to yield strength improvements remain uncertain; further microstructural analysis is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to an isothermal aging treatment at 700°C for 1 hour under an inert atmosphere and leave the other untreated. Perform elevated-temperature (up to 700°C) mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and compression) on both sets, and use electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) along with X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize microstructural changes and precipitate formation.
measurements: Yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., testing at 700°C)
Dislocation behavior and mechanical stress-strain responses
Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction (using TEM/SEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the isothermally aged samples do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength at elevated temperatures compared to the untreated samples, or if no homogeneous fine sigma precipitate formation is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In our present study, we attempted to design the new light-weight RHEAs adjusting the amount of Al content in AlxNbTiV alloys (X = 0, 0.4, 0.8, and 1). It is found that present RHEAs exhibit maintenance of single BCC phase formation with different Al contents and the Al0.8NbTiV shows the combination of high yield strength and good plasticity. Further addition of Ni or Co was made (which has larger mixing enthalpy than other constitutive alloying elements) to stimulate the formation of precipitations. It was found that the addition of Ni or Co successfully induced the formation of sigma precipitates in the BCC matrix, and it results in the enhancement of the mechanical properties at high temperatures up to 700 °C.

The heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 h on the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys results in the formation of the sigma particles within the BCC matrix. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in enhancement of yield strength in heat-treated Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys. Moreover, the high-temperature compression tests (700 and 800 °C) were conducted for the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni), and the comparison of the temperature dependence of yield strength was made via the specific yield strength (yield strength/density). The specific yield strength of the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys is superior to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718 alloy) at elevated temperatures up to 700 °C.
